extracted.intended_audience: early career researchers (aspiring peer reviewers / journal reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for early career researchers on how to perform peer review of research manuscripts for journals, including what to assess in a paper, reviewer behaviour and procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a fair, robust and timely critique
rubrics_metrics.description: When accepting the invitation to review, you are agreeing to provide a fair, robust and timely critique that is useful for the authors in improving their manuscript (whether or not the journal accepts it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure you can submit within the time frame; slow review times frustrate authors and editors may record and consider review speed when re-inviting reviewers. If you cannot meet the deadline after agreeing, contact the journal. Many journals rank reviews and invite strong reviewers again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare conflicts of interest and maintain confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have any conflicts of interest – for example, you work closely with the author or are in direct competition – you must declare these to the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts won't necessarily preclude review but must be transparent and considered by the editor. Reviews should be carried out in confidence; do not share manuscripts without editor permission. If you co-review for a supervisor or colleague, let the editor know so you can be properly credited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess originality and innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the study innovative or original? Does the study challenge existing paradigms or add to existing knowledge?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the work is novel and whether it matters in the field. High-impact journals prioritise 'ground‑breaking' work; other journals may focus on methodological validity rather than novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess clarity of the research question
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the research question clear?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear question helps judge whether the methods and analyses are appropriate and whether the results answer the question posed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess appropriateness of approach, study design, methods and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Was the approach appropriate? Are the study design, methods and analysis appropriate to the question being studied?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether chosen techniques match the question and whether the experimental or observational design can adequately address the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess reproducibility: methods described clearly enough for replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the methods described clearly enough for other researchers to replicate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for sufficient detail in protocols, materials and analytical procedures. Lack of methodological detail is a common weakness that reviewers should flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess statistical analyses and treatment of uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the statistical analyses and level of uncertainty in the data treated appropriately?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are not confident in the statistics, state your limits and inform the journal that a specialist statistical review is needed. Many journals now use or invite dedicated statistical reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess presentation of results and whether they answer the question
rubrics_metrics.description: Could the presentation of the results be improved and do they answer the question?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate figures, tables, clarity of results narrative, and whether the data support the claims made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for ethical approvals and ethical conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: If humans, human tissues or animals are involved, was ethics approval gained and was the study ethical?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag missing ethics statements or concerns to the editor. Be prepared to raise issues such as ethical oversight, conflicts of interest, plagiarism or suspected fraud; editors use COPE flowcharts to handle such issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess discussion of limitations and appropriateness of conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the discussion take into account the limitations of the study? Are the conclusions appropriate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure conclusions follow logically from the results and are not overstated; check whether authors acknowledge caveats and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess quality of data and reliability/significance of conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the quality of the data and the reliability and significance of the conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider data completeness, consistency, potential biases, and whether the conclusions are supported by robust evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge manuscript fit to journal and desk-review criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors screen submissions for relevance to the journal: format/length, clarity of discussion, research methods and overall fit with the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some journals (e.g., Nature/Science) prioritise ground‑breaking work, while others (e.g., PLOS ONE) assess only scientific and methodological validity. Understand the journal's mission when assessing suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be professional and constructive; avoid personal bias
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing, try to remember that you are an author too and be professional and constructive in your approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ad hominem remarks, personal bias or unwarranted negativity. Leave time (e.g., 24 hours) between reading and writing the review to moderate initial reactions. Judge the work, not the scientist, and be aware that knowing the authors' names can bias judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: State your expertise limits and suggest alternative reviewers where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor will not expect you to comment beyond your areas of expertise, so state any limits and suggest other reviewers if you cannot assess aspects (e.g., statistics or specialised techniques).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unable to accept an invitation, offer alternative reviewers. If asked to review outside your expertise, indicate this and request additional specialist review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and report plagiarism or possible fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewer should notify the journal office/editor if they suspect plagiarism or fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers may spot similarities to other papers, but cannot detect all plagiarism. Many journals use plagiarism-checking tools and will consult reviewers about flagged similarities. For suspected fabrication or manipulated images/data, report concerns to the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand different peer review models and their implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the differences between single-blind, double-blind and open review and the pros/cons of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-blind allows reviewer frankness but can enable unaccountable negative reviews; double-blind can reduce author-related bias but reviewers may guess authors; open review increases accountability and transparency but may reduce willingness to review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and support efficient review practices (transferable peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of transferable/cascading peer review systems where previous reviewer reports may be reused when a paper is submitted to another journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transferable review can reduce wasted reviewer effort; be open to sharing reports where appropriate and follow journal/publisher policies for transfer of reviews (e.g., Review Commons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek training, mentorship and use available resources to improve reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Most experienced reviewers learn on the job; novice reviewers should seek mentorship or training courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make use of publisher training (Elsevier, Springer Nature, Wiley, PLOS, Publons Academy, Nature Masterclasses, etc.) and ask an experienced reviewer to mentor you. Reviewing other reviewers' reports and editorial feedback helps calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek recognition and record reviewing activity appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should seek formal recognition for their work where possible and keep records of reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may publish reviewer thank-you lists; platforms such as Publons and ORCID allow public records of reviewing activity. Be cautious about payment for reviews due to potential bias concerns; many prefer non-monetary recognition (certificates, CPD points).

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt, follow journal-specific instructions and contact editors
rubrics_metrics.description: What is expected of you as a reviewer will vary from journal to journal; many journals provide online forms and specific questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure what to include in a review, contact the editorial office for guidance and follow the journal's reviewer form and policies.
